prompt: A K-map has three prime groups. Two are essential and together cover every high cell, including every cell in the third group. What should a minimum two-level cover do?

options.text: Use only the two essential groups
options.explanation: Correct. They are required and already cover all high cells.

options.text: Use all three because each is prime
options.explanation: Prime means the group cannot grow; it does not mean the group is required.

options.text: Drop an essential group to favour the third
options.explanation: An essential group uniquely covers at least one cell, which would be lost.
It does not cover the cells uniquely covered by the essential groups.

workedExample: First include each essential prime because some required row has no other prime cover. Then inspect the uncovered rows. Here none remain, so the third prime adds no logical coverage. Glitch-prevention constraints, if any, are a separate requirement.

prompt: Every high cell in a K-map belongs to two different prime groups. What follows?

options.explanation: No group uniquely covers a high cell.
High cells still need a complete cover.

options.text: There is exactly one minimum cover
options.explanation: The absence of essentials does not establish uniqueness.

options.text: No prime is essential; a covering choice is still needed
options.explanation: Correct. Without a uniquely covered cell, no particular prime is forced by the essential-prime test.

workedExample: An essential prime has a witness: a high cell covered by no other prime. None exists here. Choose a complete cover from the available primes and compare its cost; do not confuse the absence of forced groups with the absence of logic.
